text:
I need to write a reference letter. I manage a 400-cow dairy farm, and one of our workers, Tomás, is applying to the two-year agricultural technology program at the state technical college.

What I know about him:
- He's worked for us for 3 years, since he was 19.
- He runs the 3 a.m. milking shift on his own, 5 days a week.
- He learned our herd management software and now flags sick cows for the vet. Last winter he caught 9 cases of mastitis early.
- He left for 5 weeks in the middle of last summer when his father got sick in Mexico. He told me 2 days before he left.
- His written English is weaker than his spoken English. He's taking a night class for it.
- He has missed 2 shifts in 3 years, not counting those 5 weeks.

One page, from me as farm manager.

Before I draft, I have a few questions. Your answers will change what the letter says.

An admissions reader will mainly want to know whether Tomás will finish a two-year program. Your strongest evidence is the 3 a.m. shift he runs alone and his attendance record. The two things that could worry them are the written English and the 5-week absence. If I can answer those with facts, the letter will be stronger than if it leaves them out.

1. **What did his early mastitis catches save you?** For example, treatment costs, milk you didn't have to dump, or cows you kept. Even a rough figure or one specific case would help. Also, did he teach himself the software, or did you train him? This is the best evidence that he's ready for an agricultural technology program, so details matter most here.

2. **What happened with the 5-week absence?** Did he come back when he said he would? Did you hold his job, and did he help arrange cover? If he returned on time and you kept his place, the letter can mention it briefly and turn it into a point about trust. If you'd rather leave it out, tell me. The college is unlikely to ask, but I want that to be your decision.

3. **What do you know about the English night class?** Where is he taking it, how long has he been at it, and have you noticed any improvement, such as in his written log notes or reports to the vet? Admissions will notice the written-English gap in his application anyway. Showing him actively working on it makes it a point in his favor.

4. **What can you commit to?** Will he keep working for you while he studies, or would you hire him back afterward? A manager who wants him back is one of the strongest things a reference can say. I'll only include it if you can stand behind it.

5. **What does he handle on his own at 3 a.m.?** For example, calvings, equipment breakdowns, or deciding when to call you or the vet. One concrete example would show judgment as well as reliability.

6. **Names and details:** your full name and title, the farm's name and location, the college's name, and who the letter is addressed to if you know. Should it include a phone number or email for follow-up?

If you don't know an answer, just say so. I'll write around it rather than guess.

1. The vet said catching those cases early saved us about $8,000. I don't know the breakdown. Not sure on the software. I'd have to think about whether he taught himself.

2. Before he left he got his cousin, who used to work for us, to cover his shifts. He came back on the day he said he would. Fine to mention it.

3. I don't know where he's taking it or for how long. Haven't paid attention to his written notes.

4. I can keep his job open part-time on weekends while he's in the program.

5. Don't have a specific example for you.

6. Mike Hollis, farm manager, Hollis Dairy. It's for the state technical college; I don't have a name to address it to. It goes in through their online portal, due February 1. Put my phone number in: 555-0187. I'm happy to take a call from the committee.

I've written the letter from your answers. I left out anything you weren't sure of, so it doesn't say whether Tomás taught himself the software or give any details about his night class.

<final_document>
Dear Admissions Committee,

I am writing to recommend Tomás for your two-year Agricultural Technology program. I manage Hollis Dairy, a 400-cow operation. Tomás has worked for us for three years, starting at age 19. In that time he has become one of the people I rely on most.

Tomás runs our 3 a.m. milking shift on his own, five days a week. It's a demanding shift, and the herd depends on it getting done right every time. In three years he has missed two shifts. That doesn't count a family emergency, which I describe below. Your program is two years long, and showing up week after week is something he has already proven he can do.

He has also gone beyond the routine work. He learned our herd management software, and he now uses it to flag sick cows for our veterinarian. Last winter he caught nine cases of mastitis early. Our vet estimates that catching them early saved us about $8,000. Tomás already does the kind of work your program teaches: he reads the herd's data, spots a problem early and gets it to the right person.

You should also know about one absence. In the middle of last summer his father became seriously ill in Mexico, and Tomás was away for five weeks. He told me two days before he left. In those two days he got his cousin, who used to work for us, to cover his shifts. He came back on the day he said he would. In a family emergency, he made sure his work would be covered and he kept his word.

His spoken English is good. His written English is weaker, and he is taking a night class to improve it.

I will keep a part-time weekend job open for Tomás while he is in your program. I'm happy to talk with the committee about him. You can reach me at 555-0187.

Sincerely,

Mike Hollis
Farm Manager
Hollis Dairy
</final_document>

A few things to check before you upload it (due February 1):

- **Tomás's last name:** You didn't give it, so the letter only uses his first name. Add his full name to the first sentence so the college can match the letter to his application.
- **Date and college name:** I left both out because you didn't give them. Add them if the portal expects them.
- **The two days' notice:** I kept this in because it comes right before the part about him arranging cover, and the two together show how he handled the emergency. If you'd rather not mention it, delete "He told me two days before he left." Then change "In those two days" to "Before he left."
- **The software:** If you decide he did teach himself, change "He learned our herd management software" to "He taught himself our herd management software." That makes the point about him being ready for the program stronger.
